To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have: 1) constructed the largest, complete census of massive ($M \gtrapprox 10^{10.5}M_{\sun}$), slow rotator candidates in galaxy clusters, 2) confirmed that the slow rotator fraction in clusters is $\approx$ 50\%, and 3) found that the fraction of slow rotators in clusters is higher than in groups.

we have found that: (1) the kT-$Sigma$ relation is present for slow rotators in groups and clusters, (2) the fraction of slow rotators increases with stellar mass, and (3) the fraction of fast rotators is independent of environment, and is constant at 0.5.

we find that the kT-$Sigma$ relation is present in a volume-limted sample of 1,000 galaxies, and that slow rotators are found in denser environments than fast rotators, and that slow and fast rotator environments are different.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding galaxy morphology, and how this relates to the kinematics and environment of galaxies.
the kinematic morphology-density relation in galaxy clusters and groups, which we investigate in a volume-limtied sample of $\sim$ 2000 galaxies.
the kinematic morphology-density relation in the nearby universe.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the slow rotators are found in the most overdense regions, and the fast rotators are found at all densities.
the kT-$Sigma$ relation is real, but it is weak.

1) slow rotators are rare in low-density environments, but become increasingly common as density increases, 2) fast rotators are common in low-density environments and become increasingly common with increasing density, and 3) the transition between the two populations occurs at $\Sigma \sim 0.1$ Mpc$^{-2}$.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the kT-$Sigma$ relation for massive galaxies in clusters and groups is real.
we have identified 108 slow and 101 fast rotator candidates in 50 clusters and 50 galaxy groups.
we have found that the kT-$ \Sigma$ relation is similar to the morphology-$\Sigma$ one in that the fraction of slow rotators increases towards higher density.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is no evidence for a kT-$\Omega$ relation, and that slow rotators are not preferentially found in denser environments, but are found throughout the local Universe.
slow rotators are not only found in the most massive clusters, but also in groups, and are found in the outskirts of galaxy clusters.
the kT-$$\Sigma$$ relation is a tight correlation with a scatter of only $\sim 0.3$ dex, and that the slow rotator population is more tightly associated with clusters than with groups.
